q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE technological cause of accelerated globalization in the late twentieth century.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why critics argue that globalization harms workers in developed countries, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which globalization has benefited developing countries in the period c. 1900–present.

sample_answers.a: Container shipping and the internet drastically cut the cost of moving goods and coordinating production across oceans, making it economical to manufacture in one country and sell in another.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, when factories can relocate to wherever labor is cheapest, workers in wealthy countries lose bargaining power: employers threaten to move production abroad, depressing wages and eroding job security even for those who keep their jobs.
sample_answers.c: Export-oriented manufacturing has lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty in East Asia and elsewhere by providing jobs, raising incomes, and funding education and infrastructure — as in South Korea, Taiwan, and coastal China.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the late-twentieth-century wave of globalization as the result of deliberate policy choices combined with technological change. After 1980, governments slashed tariffs, deregulated finance, and built institutions like the World Trade Organization to integrate markets, while container ships, jet aircraft, and the internet made global supply chains practical. The results were double-edged. Globalization lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, especially in Asia, and gave consumers unprecedented choice. But critics argue that it also empowered mobile capital at the expense of rooted labor: corporations could pit workers in different countries against each other, environmental protections were undercut by competition for investment, and financial crises spread instantly across interconnected markets. The debate over globalization is thus a debate about who gains and who pays.
—Historian's account of globalization in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE criticism the author makes of multinational corporations.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the author connects globalization to working conditions in developing countries.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why the author's arguments resonated with protesters at the 1999 WTO meeting in Seattle.

sample_answers.a: The author argues that global brands profit by outsourcing production to contractors in poor countries, distancing themselves from the exploitation while capturing the profits — a system that rewards the evasion of responsibility.
sample_answers.b: She argues that brands dictate prices to their contractors that make decent wages impossible, while using the long subcontracting chain to deny responsibility for the workers in Jakarta or Saigon who actually make their products.
sample_answers.c: Seattle protesters — union members fearing job losses, environmentalists, and human-rights activists — found in these arguments a common language linking their different grievances to the same global economic system.

q2.stimulus:
The great multinational corporations have become increasingly detached from the actual production of the goods they sell. A brand like Nike does not make shoes; it buys them from contractors, who buy them from subcontractors, in a chain that stretches across the globe. This distance is the point: it allows the brand to claim no responsibility for the workers who stitch its products in Jakarta or Saigon, even as it dictates the prices that make decent wages impossible. Globalization, in this form, is not about sharing prosperity but about organizing its opposite — the maximum extraction of profit with the minimum of accountability.
—Adapted from Naomi Klein, No Logo, 1999

q3.directions: Use the chart below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE trend shown in the chart regarding Canada's trade as a share of GDP between 1960 and 2024.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the trend shown in the chart.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why critics of globalization would argue that the trend shown in the chart has negative consequences.

sample_answers.a: The chart shows trade (exports plus imports) rising as a share of Canada's GDP from 1960 to 2024, indicating that the Canadian economy became substantially more integrated into global markets over this period.
sample_answers.b: Trade liberalization — including the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (1988) and NAFTA (1994) — removed barriers to cross-border commerce, while falling transport and communication costs made international trade more economical.
sample_answers.c: Critics would argue that deeper trade integration exposed Canadian workers to competition from lower-wage countries, pressured governments to weaken labor and environmental standards to attract investment, and made the economy vulnerable to distant financial shocks.

q3.stimulus: The chart, from Our World in Data (Creative Commons BY license), shows trade — the combined value of exports and imports — as a share of GDP for Canada from 1960 to 2024. The line trends upward across the period, with trade growing from a smaller fraction of the economy in the 1960s to a substantially larger share by the 2020s, illustrating Canada's deepening integration into the global economy.
